summary.title: Incident Review and Postmortem Best Practices
summary.one_liner: You learn how companies run incident response and postmortems, the practices that stand out, and newer ideas such as focusing on learning over action-item tracking and taking a socio-technical view instead of the Five Whys.
keywords: how to run a postmortem meeting
takeaways: Most companies follow a common incident flow: detection, declaration, mitigation, decompression, analysis/postmortem, review, and follow-up actions.
Good practices include encouraging early incident declaration, defining roles such as Incident Commander, setting severity levels ahead of time, and keeping playbooks handy.
Run blameless reviews that look at why systems allowed a change without feedback, and separate accountability from blame.
Structure review meetings: prepare upfront, level set, walk through the timeline, recognize what went well, and consider splitting learning and action-item meetings.
The Five Whys can miss other root causes; a socio-technical approach looks at both technical failures and how the incident was handled.
summary.summary: This Pragmatic Engineer newsletter article surveys how more than 60 teams handle outages, describing a common incident lifecycle and the tooling and less common practices they mention. It then lays out incident handling best practices, such as blameless reviews, structured review meetings, and clear incident roles, with input from incident.io and Jeli. The article also covers newer approaches: Honeycomb's shift away from templates and action-item tracking, critiques of the Five Whys, and John Allspaw's view that tech can learn from other industries. The author uses interviews and quotes throughout rather than step-by-step instructions.
